content: The hepatitis C virus (HCV) core antigen (cAg) assay is designed to break down viral particles, expose the antigen, and separate antibodies from the antigen to enhance the detection of HCV cAg. This process is critical for improving diagnostic accuracy. Equity, Ethics, and Human Rights Implications The decentralization of HCV testing is expected to improve equity by increasing access to testing in underserved areas. Variability in access to treatment across regions and countries remains a concern. Ethical considerations include the potential for the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend suboptimal testing strategies, which could either improve or reduce equity depending on the context. Resource Use and Financial Implications The implementation of HCV testing requires investment in testing platforms, reagents, and other laboratory consumables. Training laboratory staff and ensuring quality control are essential, particularly when using near point-of-care (POC) assays. Costs associated with testing vary depending on the type of assay and the resources available in different settings. Feasibility challenges include regional disparities in access to testing equipment and services, as well as the availability of local laboratories capable of procuring necessary materials. Feasibility and Implementation Constraints Major barriers to implementing HCV testing include regional and country-specific differences in access to treatment and testing infrastructure. The availability of local laboratories equipped to perform HCV cAg testing is critical. The feasibility of implementation depends on the context, with some settings requiring significant stakeholder involvement and resource allocation. Relevance to Populations HCV cAg testing is particularly relevant for populations relying on centralized laboratory testing for HCV RNA confirmation. However, in high-income settings with established hepatitis C testing and treatment programs, these recommendations may be less applicable. Research Gaps Further research is needed to evaluate the kinetics of HCV cAg during treatment, especially with new direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens. Studies should also assess covariates such as HIV or HBV co-infection and genotype in the context of HCV cAg or nucleic acid tests (NATs) for treatment monitoring or cure confirmation. Additionally, the necessity and optimal timing of treatment monitoring and cure confirmation with DAA regimens require further investigation. The development of multiplex diagnostic instruments capable of detecting other diseases like HIV, HBV, and tuberculosis (TB) alongside HCV is also a priority. Background and Global Burden Globally, approximately 250 million people are chronically infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV), and 80–140 million are infected with chronic HCV. Chronic HBV and HCV infections account for over 90% of deaths related to viral hepatitis, making it the seventh leading cause of mortality worldwide. Advances in antiviral therapies have significantly improved the clinical management of HBV and HCV, with HCV increasingly becoming curable. However, achieving the full benefits of these therapies requires a comprehensive continuum of care, starting with screening and extending to sustained viral suppression. Barriers to Screening Barriers to hepatitis screening include a lack of knowledge and awareness, limited access to screening infrastructure, cultural beliefs, financial constraints, fear of blood tests, and stigma. Addressing these barriers is essential to improving the management of chronic viral hepatitis. Interventions to Improve Screening and Linkage to Care Educational interventions targeting healthcare workers and patients have been shown to increase knowledge about hepatitis, improve screening rates, and enhance treatment adherence. Clinician reminders and quality improvement initiatives have also demonstrated effectiveness in increasing hepatitis screening and linkage to care. However, challenges such as stigma and limited access to healthcare services in resource-poor settings must be addressed. Ethical and Equity Considerations Increasing hepatitis B and C screening rates is expected to enhance equity by improving access to care and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. Resource Use and Cost-Effectiveness Scaling up testing and treatment programs can reduce the burden of advanced liver disease, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and related complications, ultimately decreasing premature morbidity and mortality. However, the cost of implementing new systems, such as electronic health records for clinician reminders, may pose financial challenges. Implementation Considerations Simple educational interventions and clinician reminders are highly feasible and cost-effective. Coordinated mental health and substance abuse services within HCV care delivery can improve treatment outcomes and prevent further transmission. Stakeholder involvement is crucial for successful implementation. Research Needs There is an urgent need for implementation research, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), to optimize chronic viral hepatitis service delivery systems. Costing studies and evaluations of interventions to improve screening, linkage to care, and treatment adherence are also necessary. Conclusion Hepatitis B and C screening and treatment programs are essential for reducing the global burden of viral hepatitis. Addressing barriers to care, improving equity, and conducting further research will be critical to achieving better health outcomes for affected populations.
